stem.en: The epithelial tissues that line many internal organs, such as the lungs and the blood vessels, are usually only one or a few cells thick. Why?

text.en: To allow quick exchange of materials across them.

feedback.en: Yes. A thin lining gives materials only a short distance to cross, so they pass through quickly.

text.en: To give the organ as much strength as possible against pulling and pressure.

feedback.en: No. One thin layer of cells is not strong. Strength and support come from connective tissues such as bone.

text.en: To store food in the lining, so that the organ always has a supply of energy.

feedback.en: No. Storing food is not a job of these thin linings. Their job is to let materials pass across.

text.en: To reduce friction when food or air rubs against the inside of the organ.

feedback.en: No. Protection from friction comes from many layers of cells, as in the skin, mouth and oesophagus. A thin lining does the opposite job: it lets materials through.

explanation.en: A lining that is one or a few cells thick gives materials only a short distance to cross. In the lungs, oxygen passes from the air into the blood through a single layer of thin, flat cells, so it gets across quickly. Many layers of cells, as in the skin, are found where protection is needed instead.

hints.en: Think of the lining of the lungs. What has to pass across it?
Is a short distance or a long distance quicker to cross?
